newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Cuban cigars "forbidden fruit" in U.S. smoking fad.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cuban cigars "forbidden fruit" in U.S. smoking fad.

text.p: The names alone make cigar lovers drool -- Cohiba, Montecristo, Partagas.
But while a craze for cigar smoking has more and more Americans lighting up, the legendary cigars of Cuba are banned under a U.S. embargo against the communist-ruled island.
The result, customs officers and industry sources say, is a dramatic rise in smuggling and counterfeiting.
"Cuban cigars are the forbidden fruit of cigar aficionados," said Michael Sheehan, spokesman for the U.S. Customs Service in Miami.
"If you can't have something, that makes the allure much greater. We're seeing more smuggling of Cuban cigars because of the popularity of cigar smoking in the United States."
Some smugglers run boats across the Florida Straits from Havana to the Keys. Many people, professionals among them, try to pack a box or two in their luggage from foreign trips.
It is not necessary to travel to Cuba to get the prized smoke. As no other country maintains the embargo, they can be bought openly in Canada, Europe or Latin America.
Once they reach the United States, however, the price rises. A Cohiba which costs $3 in Havana will sell for $25 in Miami and as much as $50 in New York, Sheehan said.
"A lot of people come in here asking for Cuban cigars," said Angel Bernal, who rolls and sells his own cigars at his Smokers' Road shop in Miami's Little Havana district.
"A lot of people want to sell me some too. Doctors, lawyers, even.
"It's tempting because of the money but for me it's not worth it," he hastened to add. "Everybody knows about the embargo. It's like Prohibition days. They know it's illegal but they still want it."
BIG RISE IN CONFISCATED CIGARS

The Treasury Department has sent letters to members of the Retail Tobacco Dealers of America warning them against dealing in Cuban cigars. U.S. Customs figures show a big increase in seizures this year.
The estimated domestic value of cigars seized rose from about $142,000 in 1994 to more than a million dollars this year. The number of cigars seized was 96,216 in 1996 compared to 24,360 in 1994.
Most were picked up at New York's J.F.Kennedy airport -- more than $530,000 worth. About $92,000 worth were seized at Miami airport and $66,000 at the seaport.
"They are more opportunists than career criminals or drug smugglers," Sheehan said.
But some smugglers are aiming for the big time, he said.

In August, the U.S. Coast Guard seized 122 boxes containing 3,016 cigars in a 29-foot (nine-metre) powerboat as it returned to the United States from the Bahamas heading for Fort Lauderdale. They were worth about $57,000 in south Florida and possibly double that in New York.

The same month, customs officers in Key West nabbed Richard Sperandino as he unloaded his fishing boat. They found 111 boxes with 2,700 cigars. Sperandino said he bought them in Cuba for $3,600 and could sell them for $28,000. He led agents to a warehouse in New York packed with Cuban cigars.
BOOM IN COUNTERFEITING
The lust for Cuban cigars has also brought a boom in counterfeiting.
"A lot of Cuban people in Hialeah (a Hispanic district of Miami) know the art. They make them there and sell them down in South Beach," Bernal said.

"Buy a $3 dollar cigar, take off the wrapper, print up your own label and reseal it. It's much easier and less risky than smuggling and many alleged aficionados have no idea what they are smoking," Sheehan said.
Many other fakes are made in the Dominican Republic, which has excellent cigars of its own.
The mystique of Cuban cigars prevails in the glossy magazines and smart clubs which cater to the fashion.
"Everybody says "I want a Cohiba'," said Frank Sulita, maitre d'hotel of the Cuba Club, a discreet Miami Beach haunt of dark polished wood, leather chairs and good whisky to go with the smokes.
Celebrities such as Michael Caine and Madonna keep their own collections in a side room where humidors with brass name plates line the walls like boxes in a bank vault.
Asked about the availablity of Cuban cigars, Sulita said: "I don't want to know about it. I don't want people in here bragging about Cubans."
Busting cigar smokers, however, was not on the Miami police list of priorities, Sheehan said.
"Cigars are cigars. Heroin is heroin. There is a difference. But we still take the embargo seriously."
